propositions.text: The EU AI Act applies a risk-based framework with four tiers plus a parallel regime for general-purpose AI models.

The first tier is prohibited practices: Article 5 bans eight categories of AI practice outright, including subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement except in narrowly defined circumstances, and others.

The second tier is high-risk systems, reached by two cumulative routes under Article 6: a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, or where the system falls within one of the use-case categories listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration, and administration of justice.

The third tier is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency obligations, which require providers to ensure natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, to mark synthetic audio, image, video or text content in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated, and require deployers to inform persons exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems and to disclose deepfake content.
The fourth tier is minimal risk, for which the Regulation imposes no mandatory obligations.

Running parallel to these four tiers is the general-purpose AI model regime under Articles 51 to 56: Article 51 classifies a general-purpose AI model as having systemic risk where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, or where the Commission so designates it; Article 53 sets baseline provider duties for all general-purpose AI models; and Article 55 adds further obligations for those with systemic risk.

propositions.text: The Regulation supplies risk criteria at two levels: criteria for classifying a system as high-risk in the first place, and criteria for managing risk once a system is classified as high-risk.
For classification, Article 7 sets out the factors the Commission must consider when assessing whether an Annex III use case poses a significant risk of harm.
The factors include the intended purpose of the AI system.
The factors include the extent to which it has been or is likely to be used.
The factors include the nature and amount of data processed, including whether special categories of personal data are involved.
The factors include the degree of autonomy and the possibility for a human to override its outputs.
The factors include the extent to which use of the system has already caused harm to health, safety or fundamental rights or given rise to significant concerns.
The factors include the potential extent of such harm in terms of its intensity and its ability to affect multiple persons or to disproportionately affect a particular group.

For ongoing risk management once a system is high-risk, Article 9 requires the provider to establish, implement, document and maintain a continuous iterative risk management system across the entire lifecycle of the system.
The risk management system comprises identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights.
The risk management system comprises estimation and evaluation of risks arising from intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse.
The risk management system comprises evaluation of risks arising from post-market monitoring data.
The risk management system comprises adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures to address identified risks.
Article 9 further requires that residual risks associated with each hazard, and the overall residual risk of the system, be judged acceptable and communicated to the deployer.

The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It shall comprise the following steps: (a) the identification and analysis of the known and the reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose; (b) the estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose, and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse; (c) the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72; (d) the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified pursuant to point (a).

propositions.text: The EU AI Act applies a risk-based framework with four tiers plus a parallel regime for general-purpose AI models.

The first tier is prohibited practices: Article 5 bans eight categories of AI practice outright, including subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement except in narrowly defined circumstances, and others.

The second tier is high-risk systems, reached by two cumulative routes under Article 6: a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, or where the system falls within one of the use-case categories listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration, and administration of justice.

The third tier is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency obligations, which require providers to ensure natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, to mark synthetic audio, image, video or text content in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated, and require deployers to inform persons exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems and to disclose deepfake content.
The fourth tier is minimal risk, for which the Regulation imposes no mandatory obligations.

Running parallel to these four tiers is the general-purpose AI model regime under Articles 51 to 56: Article 51 classifies a general-purpose AI model as having systemic risk where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, or where the Commission so designates it; Article 53 sets baseline provider duties for all general-purpose AI models; and Article 55 adds further obligations for those with systemic risk.
